lead: A dual-fuel engine burns two fuels in the same cycle: a gas that carries most of the energy, and a small diesel pilot that lights it. Methane and most gas fuels have a cetane number near zero, so compression alone does not ignite them in the time the piston allows; the pilot supplies the ignition. A multi-fuel engine is something else: one engine that runs on any one of several fuels, one at a time. Dual fuel is used in CNG and biogas gensets, converted trucks and LNG ships; multi-fuel in military and farm engines.
prereq: You need: ignition delay and diesel knock (Combustion in SI and CI engines), and the gas fuels of alternative fuels.

sections.h3: Three terms that are not the same

head: Term
What burns in the cylinder
Example
rows: gas and a diesel pilot together, every cycle
one fuel at a time, switched by the driver or controller
any one of a range of liquid fuels, one at a time
military truck diesel running diesel, kerosene or jet fuel

blocks.text: In a dual-fuel engine the gas does most of the work and the diesel only lights it. A bi-fuel car carries two fuels but never burns them together. A multi-fuel engine promises fuel flexibility, not a mixture of fuels.

sections.h3: Metering the gas and lighting it

blocks.text: The gas is mixed with the air before the intake valve, which is called fumigation. A venturi mixer draws gas in with the pressure drop at its throat; a gas carburettor adds a zero-pressure regulator and a metering valve; timed port injection through solenoid gas injectors gives the best control and the least risk of backfire in the manifold. The cycle then runs:

items: A lean gas–air charge enters and is compressed.

At a compression ratio of about 17 the charge reaches roughly 800 to 860 K, near methane’s self-ignition temperature of about 810 K, but at that temperature methane takes far longer to ignite than the few milliseconds the piston stays near top dead centre.
A small diesel pilot is injected near top dead centre. Diesel has a short delay, so it ignites first.
The burning pilot sprays act like many spark plugs and start flames through the gas–air charge; expansion follows as in a diesel.

blocks.text: The pilot is quoted as its share of the fuel energy. In converted truck and genset diesels it is often 10 to 30 per cent at high load and more at light load; large purpose-built gas engines use a micro-pilot of about 1 per cent. A common-rail injector can meter such a small pilot accurately; a mechanical pump cannot go much below its idle delivery.

sections.h3: Substitution, knock and the light-load penalty

blocks.text: Two figures describe how much diesel the gas replaces. The diesel substitution is the share of the diesel mass saved: (ṁd − ṁdf) ÷ ṁd, where ṁd is the diesel flow on diesel alone and ṁdf the pilot flow in dual-fuel mode at the same power. The gas energy share is ṁgLHVg ÷ (ṁgLHVg + ṁdfLHVd), where ṁg is the gas flow. They differ because the efficiency of the engine changes when gas is used.

At high load the gas share and the premixed charge are largest. If the pilot is early, the intake hot or the compression ratio high, the end gas ignites before the flames arrive: knock. Methane’s high octane number delays it, but knock still caps the substitution at full load.

At light load the gas–air charge is very lean. Flames from the pilot travel slowly and die in the leanest parts, so some gas leaves unburnt: CO and HC rise and the efficiency falls. The unburnt methane is called methane slip. It comes mainly from this incomplete burning, from crevices and quench layers, and partly from fresh charge that short-circuits to the exhaust during valve overlap. Methane warms the climate far more per kg than CO2, so slip matters more than its HC number suggests.

A multi-fuel engine is a diesel built to accept fuels of different ignition quality. Its compression ratio is fixed at build, so it is a compromise: high enough (often above 20) for a low-cetane fuel to ignite, but limited by peak pressure. The injection pump must deliver the same energy from fuels of different density and viscosity; some military engines used a fuel-density compensator on the pump for this. Four properties set the fuel range: cetane number (ignition delay and knock), viscosity (spray and pump leakage), lubricity (pump and injector wear) and volatility (vapour lock in a hot pump).

Producer-gas dual fuel is the classic rural set: a biomass gasifier feeds a diesel genset. Producer gas has a low heating value and is about half nitrogen, so the engine is derated and the pilot share stays high, often a third of the energy or more.

examples.question: A dual-fuel engine gives 40 kW. On diesel alone it burns 10 kg/h. At the same power in dual-fuel mode it burns 2.5 kg/h of diesel (LHV 42.5 MJ/kg) and 6.6 kg/h of CNG (LHV 50 MJ/kg). Find the diesel substitution, the gas energy share and the brake thermal efficiency in both modes.
steps: Dual-fuel energies: diesel 2.5 × 42.5 = 106.25 MJ/h; gas 6.6 × 50 = 330 MJ/h; total 436.25 MJ/h.
Brake power in MJ/h: 40 kW × 3.6 = 144 MJ/h.
examples.answer: The gas replaces 75 % of the diesel mass and supplies 75.6 % of the energy; efficiency falls slightly, from 33.9 % to 33.0 %.

traps: Mixing up the definitions: diesel saved (75 % above), gas energy share (75.6 %) and gas mass share (6.6 ÷ 9.1 = 72.5 %) are three different numbers; say which one you give.
Calling a CNG-petrol car dual fuel: it is bi-fuel, the fuels are switched, never burnt together.
Treating the pilot as a fixed 10 %: it is set at each operating point, larger at light load.
Assuming more gas is always better: at light load it brings CO, HC and methane slip; at high load, knock.
Saying methane slip comes only from valve overlap: most of it is gas the lean flames never burnt.

quiz.q: Define a dual-fuel engine in one sentence.
quiz.a: An engine in which a gaseous fuel that carries most of the energy is burnt, every cycle, together with a small diesel pilot that ignites it.

quiz.q: What is a bi-fuel vehicle? Give an example.
quiz.a: A vehicle that carries two fuels and runs on one at a time, such as a CNG-petrol car.

quiz.q: Why will a diesel engine of compression ratio 17 not run on methane alone?
quiz.a: The compressed charge is only about at methane’s self-ignition temperature, and methane’s ignition delay there is much longer than the time near top dead centre; a pilot gives a quick-igniting source instead.

quiz.q: On diesel alone an engine burns 8 kg/h. In dual-fuel mode it burns 2 kg/h of diesel (42.5 MJ/kg) and 4 kg/h of gas (50 MJ/kg). Find the diesel substitution and the gas energy share.
quiz.a: Substitution (8 − 2) ÷ 8 = 75 %. Energies: diesel 85 MJ/h, gas 200 MJ/h, total 285 MJ/h; gas share 200 ÷ 285 = 70.2 %.

quiz.q: Name three fuel properties that limit a multi-fuel engine and say what each affects.
quiz.a: Cetane number (ignition delay and knock), viscosity (spray and pump leakage) and lubricity (pump and injector wear); volatility also matters for vapour lock.

quiz.q: Why does dual-fuel efficiency fall at light load while knock appears at high load?
quiz.a: At light load the gas–air charge is very lean, flames are slow and die out, so gas leaves unburnt (CO, HC, slip) and efficiency drops. At high load the premixed charge is large and hot, and the end gas can self-ignite before the flames reach it.

quiz.q: A genset at 25 % load shows high CO and methane in the exhaust. Suggest two changes.
quiz.a: Reduce the gas share and enlarge the pilot, so the flames start from more sites; and make the charge less lean, by throttling the air or using hot EGR, so the flames travel faster and burn more of the gas.

beyond: Not for the exam. LNG dual-fuel engines are now common in ships, and methanol and ammonia dual-fuel engines are coming because these low-cetane fuels need the same pilot idea. Shipping rules now count methane slip as a greenhouse emission, so pilot strategy and slip measurement are active work. Search next for “high-pressure direct injection of natural gas”, “methane slip” and “micro-pilot ignition”.
